title: The Emptied Capital
subtitle: The yellow fever epidemic in Philadelphia, August–November 1793
intro: In late August 1793 a fever began killing people along the Water Street wharves of Philadelphia, then the capital of the United States and its largest city, with about 50,000 people. By the time cold weather ended it in November, Mathew Carey had counted 4,041 named dead; later estimates put the toll near 5,000, roughly one resident in ten. About a third of the city fled, the President among them. The federal government dispersed, the banks closed, and a mayor with a committee of volunteers kept the city running.

Almost none of the record is a diary. The heart of this chapter is a run of more than fifty letters Benjamin Rush wrote to his wife, nearly every day, from the city's busiest sickrooms, printed in 1892. Around them stand dated letters by Jefferson, Hamilton and Washington; a Quaker matron's diary of names; a Lutheran pastor's account built from his journal; the committee's minutes; and four printed accounts written in the aftermath by Carey, Rush, the refugee physician Jean Devèze, and Absalom Jones and Richard Allen. The form tags say which is which, and Samuel Breck's recollections, written decades later, are marked as memory.

The physicians did not agree on anything that mattered. Rush thought the fever was bred locally from putrid matter, perhaps a spoiled cargo of coffee, and treated it with huge purges of calomel and jalap and repeated bleeding. The College of Physicians and Carey thought it had been imported from the West Indies, where refugees from the revolution in Saint-Domingue had sailed from that summer. Devèze, who had treated the fever in the Caribbean, thought it local but not contagious, and treated it gently. Hamilton credited his recovery to a West Indian treatment of bark and cold baths, and the choice of cure took on party colours. These are given as positions. A century later the mosquito Aedes aegypti was shown to carry the disease, which explains both the ships and the frost.

The heaviest work fell to Black Philadelphians. Rush, wrongly believing they were largely spared, urged Jones and Allen to help; they and their community nursed, bled and buried through the worst weeks, and 305 Black people were buried that year against 67 the year before. When Carey's pamphlet accused some Black nurses of extortion and plunder, Jones and Allen answered in print with names and accounts. Nurses such as the widow Sarah Bass, and Rush's servant Marcus, who nursed him through his relapse, appear only in others' pages: no surviving firsthand account by them has been found.

Read across, the eyes show the same weeks as a medical crusade, a list of neighbours' names, a divine judgment, a constitutional problem and a test of who would serve. The death counts are other people's counts, each made by a different method, and they are labelled by whose they are.
calendar_note: All dates are Gregorian and need no conversion. Rush often wrote one letter over two days, and a few printed summaries disagree by a day about postscripts; such entries are marked as ranges. Carey's first-edition preface (13 November 1793) and his later editions differ in text, so quotations are tied to the edition seen.

eyes.name: Benjamin Rush
eyes.role: Physician, aged 47; professor at the University of Pennsylvania, signer of the Declaration of Independence
eyes.where: His house on Walnut Street, and the sickrooms of the city
eyes.vantage_label: the physician at the centre of the storm
eyes.form: dated letters, and a published account (1794)
eyes.authenticity: His near-daily letters to his wife Julia, who was in New Jersey with most of the children, survive at Duke University (Rubenstein Library) and were first printed in 'Old Family Letters Relating to the Yellow Fever' (1892); the standard edition is Butterfield's 'Letters of Benjamin Rush' (1951). His 'Account of the Bilious Remitting Yellow Fever' (1794) is a retrospective treatise, argued in his own favour.
eyes.bio: Rush identified the epidemic in mid-August, stayed in the city throughout, and staked his reputation on massive purging with calomel and jalap and on heavy bleeding. His letters to Julia are the closest thing to a diary the epidemic produced: patient counts, the deaths of his pupils and his sister, his own repeated illness, and a running quarrel with colleagues. He believed the fever was generated locally from putrid matter and was not imported.

sources.title: Old Family Letters Relating to the Yellow Fever (Philadelphia: Lippincott, 1892), NLM digitised text
Duke University, Benjamin and Julia Stockton Rush papers (letter of 25–26 Aug 1793)
Penn Libraries guide: Rush and Yellow Fever (list of the 56 letters)
Rush, An Account of the Bilious Remitting Yellow Fever (1794), NLM

eyes.name: Absalom Jones and Richard Allen
eyes.role: Formerly enslaved Methodist preachers and leaders of the Free African Society; Jones aged about 47, Allen 33
eyes.side: Black Philadelphians; the Free African Society
eyes.where: Black neighbourhoods of the southern city; the sickrooms and burial grounds
eyes.form: published narrative (January 1794), written with dated accounts
eyes.authenticity: Their 'Narrative of the Proceedings of the Black People, during the Late Awful Calamity' was entered for copyright on 23 January 1794 and printed with a certificate from Mayor Clarkson. It is a jointly written reply to Mathew Carey, so it is both testimony and argument. They are treated here as one eye because the record is a single joint text.
eyes.bio: Asked in early September to help, Jones and Allen organised Black Philadelphians to nurse the sick, carry the dead and bury them, and, trained by Rush, bled hundreds of patients. When Carey's pamphlet singled out Black nurses for extortion and theft, they answered with names, numbers and an account of their own losses. Theirs is the only first-hand record from the people who did the heaviest work of the epidemic.

sources.title: Jones and Allen, A Narrative of the Proceedings of the Black People (1794), NLM digitised text
NPS, Absalom Jones and Richard Allen on the yellow fever

eyes.name: Mathew Carey
eyes.role: Irish-born printer and publisher, aged 33; member of the citizens' relief committee
eyes.side: Philadelphia printers and the Mayor's committee
eyes.where: Philadelphia; committee rooms at City Hall
eyes.authenticity: The first edition's preface and copyright are dated 13 November 1793; prefaces to the second and third editions are dated 23 and 30 November, and the fourth edition, 'improved', is dated 16 January 1794 and carries a list of 4,041 names of the dead. Text changed between editions, including the passage on Black nurses that Jones and Allen answered.
eyes.bio: Carey sat on the relief committee and rushed out the first history of the epidemic while it was ending, a best-seller that went through four editions in two months. He compiled the death toll from church books and house-to-house inquiry. He held that the fever had been imported from the West Indies. His charge that some Black nurses extorted and plundered set off the first printed answer by Black authors to a public slur in American history.

sources.title: Carey, A Short Account of the Malignant Fever, 4th ed. (16 Jan 1794), NLM digitised text
Carey, Short Account (NLM catalogue)

eyes.name: Matthew Clarkson
eyes.role: Mayor of Philadelphia, about 60; chairman of the citizens' relief committee
eyes.form: official record: proclamations, letters and committee minutes
eyes.authenticity: The committee's daily minutes survive in manuscript (Historical Society of Pennsylvania; Library Company) and were printed as 'Minutes of the Proceedings of the Committee, Appointed on the 14th September, 1793' (Philadelphia: R. Aitken, 1794). His orders and addresses are known through newspapers and Carey's dated summaries.
eyes.bio: With the state and federal governments gone and most of the city council fled, Clarkson remained and improvised a government out of volunteers. His committee borrowed money, took over Bush Hill, opened an orphan house, hired carts and coffins, and counted the dead. He signed the certificate that vouched for Jones and Allen's conduct.

sources.title: Minutes of the Proceedings of the Committee (1794), Duke exhibit
Library Company finding aid, committee minutes 1793–94
HSP primary source: Committee to Attend to the Malignant Fever, minutes

eyes.name: Stephen Girard
eyes.role: French-born merchant and shipowner, aged 43; volunteer manager of the Bush Hill fever hospital
eyes.side: Merchant community; French émigrés; the Mayor's committee
eyes.where: Bush Hill hospital, north-west of the city
eyes.authenticity: Girard's letterbooks are in the Girard Papers at Girard College; most 1793 letters are in French and were not consulted for this chapter. His Bush Hill work is recorded in the committee minutes and in the testimony of Carey and Devèze; entries built from those are marked as such.
eyes.bio: On 15 September Girard and the merchant Peter Helm offered to take charge of Bush Hill, a mansion seized as a hospital that had become a place of neglect. Girard nursed patients with his own hands for weeks and hired the French physician Devèze. A man of business rather than of letters, he is seen here mostly through the papers of others.

sources.title: Devèze, Enquiry into ... the Epidemic Disease (1794), NLM
Carey, A Short Account of the Malignant Fever, 4th ed. (16 Jan 1794), NLM digitised text

eyes.name: Jean Devèze
eyes.role: French physician, about 40, a refugee from Cap-Français in Saint-Domingue; physician at Bush Hill
eyes.form: published treatise (1794), French with English translation
eyes.authenticity: His 'Recherches et observations sur les causes et les effets de la maladie épidémique' was printed in Philadelphia by Parent in 1794 with a facing English translation. It is retrospective and argumentative but rests on his Bush Hill cases and autopsies.
eyes.bio: Devèze reached Philadelphia on the brig Mary from Cap-Français shortly before the outbreak, part of the wave of refugees from the revolution in Saint-Domingue. At Bush Hill he treated patients cautiously, with limited bleeding and none of Rush's heavy purging, and opened many bodies. He argued that the fever was epidemic but not contagious, and he is the clearest voice of the West Indian clinical tradition in this chapter.

sources.title: Devèze, Enquiry (1794), NLM digitised text
Wellcome Collection copy

eyes.name: Elizabeth Sandwith Drinker
eyes.role: Quaker matron, aged 58, wife of the merchant Henry Drinker
eyes.where: Philadelphia and its outskirts; the family also kept a summer house near Frankford
eyes.authenticity: Her diary of 1758–1807 is at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania. Extracts were printed by Henry D. Biddle in 1889, and the full edition by Elaine Forman Crane in 1991. Entries here come from published extracts and quoted passages; where she was on each day is not settled in this chapter.
eyes.bio: Drinker's diary is a ledger of hearsay death: day after day she wrote down the names of neighbours and Friends reported dead, and the rumours about the cause. She is the steady voice of the households that waited, counted and prayed while the physicians argued.

sources.title: HSP, Elizabeth Sandwith Drinker diary
Philadelphia Yearly Meeting: Quakers and the yellow fever of 1793

eyes.name: Justus Henry Christian Helmuth
eyes.role: German Lutheran pastor of St Michael's and Zion, aged 48
eyes.side: German Lutheran congregation, the city's hardest-hit church
eyes.where: Lutheran parish, Fourth and Cherry Streets
eyes.form: published account (1793) drawing on his journal
eyes.authenticity: His 'Kurze Nachricht von dem sogenannten gelben Fieber in Philadelphia' (1793) was translated by Charles Erdmann as 'A Short Account of the Yellow Fever in Philadelphia, for the Reflecting Christian' (1794). It quotes dated passages from his own journal; the manuscript journal was not consulted.
eyes.bio: Helmuth stayed and visited the sick of a largely poor, German-speaking congregation that buried more of the dead than any other in the city. He read the epidemic as a just and merciful God's punishment and recorded the collapse of funeral custom. His is the immigrant church's view of the plague year.

sources.title: Helmuth, A Short Account of the Yellow Fever (1794), NLM digitised text

eyes.name: Thomas Jefferson
eyes.where: A rented house on the Schuylkill outside the city, then Monticello
eyes.vantage_label: cabinet officer on the city's edge
eyes.authenticity: Letters to Madison and others are edited in 'The Papers of Thomas Jefferson' vol. 27 and on Founders Online.
eyes.bio: Jefferson kept riding into the emptying city to work while sending his daughter away, and his letters to Madison give death counts, rumours and politics in the same breath, including a sneer at Hamilton's illness. He left for Virginia in mid-September.

sources.title: Jefferson to Madison, 1 Sept 1793 (Founders Online)
Jefferson to Madison, 12 Sept 1793 (Founders Online)
Poplar Forest: Jefferson's response to the epidemic

eyes.name: Alexander Hamilton
eyes.role: Secretary of the Treasury, in his late thirties; patient
eyes.where: His house in Philadelphia, then Albany
eyes.authenticity: His open letter to the College of Physicians appeared in the Federal Gazette on 11 September 1793; it is edited in 'The Papers of Alexander Hamilton' vol. 15 and on Founders Online.
eyes.bio: Hamilton and his wife Elizabeth both caught the fever in early September and were treated by his boyhood friend from St Croix, Dr Edward Stevens, with bark, wine and cold baths rather than Rush's purges. Hamilton published his recovery as an endorsement, and the choice of cure became a party question.

sources.title: Hamilton to the College of Physicians, [11 Sept 1793] (Founders Online)
Washington to Hamilton, 6 Sept 1793 (Founders Online)

eyes.name: George Washington
eyes.role: President of the United States, aged 61
eyes.where: The President's House on Market Street, then Mount Vernon, then Germantown
eyes.authenticity: Letters edited in 'The Papers of George Washington, Presidential Series' vol. 14 and on Founders Online.
eyes.bio: Washington left on 10 September with his household, at Martha's urging, and governed by post from Mount Vernon, where his worry was where and whether Congress could lawfully meet in December. His secretary Tobias Lear had lost his wife Polly to a fever that summer.

sources.title: Washington to Hamilton, 25 Sept 1793 (Founders Online)
Washington to Madison, 14 Oct 1793 (Founders Online)
Colonial Williamsburg: Washington and the 1793 epidemic

eyes.name: Samuel Breck
eyes.where: Bristol on the Delaware, and Philadelphia on business
eyes.authenticity: 'Recollections of Samuel Breck, with Passages from his Note-Books', edited by H. E. Scudder (1877), written decades after the events. Some details are misremembered, for example a hard frost on 12 October ending the epidemic, which the contemporary records do not support.
eyes.bio: Breck followed his family to Bristol in late August but went back into the city in September to load a ship for Liverpool. His memoir gives the street scenes that letters left out, filtered through old age.

sources.title: Breck, Recollections, excerpt (Minnesota State OER)

entries.place: At sea from Cap-Français to Philadelphia
entries.headline: Refugees from Saint-Domingue reach the Delaware
entries.digest: Devèze sailed on the brig Mary from Cap-Français, which was in flames and upheaval, among the refugees arriving in Philadelphia that summer. He later stressed that no one aboard had fever on the voyage, though pirates had seized the passengers' goods. The city raised about $12,000 for the newcomers.
entries.source_note: Devèze, Enquiry (1794), opening section; refugee relief figure from Carey, 4th ed. Day of arrival not given.

entries.headline: Naming the fever at a dying woman's bedside
entries.digest: Called in consultation with Drs Hodge and Foulke to Catherine LeMaigre near the Water Street wharves, Rush saw a fever he linked to the cases of the past fortnight and to the 1762 epidemic of his youth. He declared it the bilious remitting yellow fever and told colleagues it was spreading. The woman died the next day.
entries.source_note: Rush, Account (1794); American Heritage, '1793: Two Hundred Years Ago'. Carey dates Mrs LeMaigre's death 20 Aug.

entries.headline: A summons to a sick man who is dead by morning
entries.digest: Helmuth was called to a man on 19 August who was dead on the 20th, and another death followed in the same family on the 21st. A ship's carpenter he buried in Kensington was dead by the 25th. In retrospect he took these as the opening of the visitation.
entries.source_note: Helmuth, Short Account (Erdmann trans., 1794), NLM text.

entries.headline: The first deaths the town talks about
entries.digest: Carey later fixed the first death to attract general notice as Peter Aston's on 19 August, followed by Mrs LeMaigre on the 20th and Thomas Miller on the 25th. In his telling the alarm spread only once Rush and others spoke of a malignant fever.
entries.source_note: Carey, A Short Account of the Malignant Fever, 4th ed. (16 Jan 1794), NLM digitised text.

entries.headline: Warning Julia to stay away
entries.digest: Rush wrote to his wife that a malignant fever had broken out in Water Street between Arch and Race and had already killed twelve. He asked her to stay where she was until he sent word. It was the first of more than fifty letters he wrote her through the epidemic.
entries.quote: a malignant fever has broken out in Water Street
entries.source_note: Old Family Letters Relating to the Yellow Fever (Philadelphia: Lippincott, 1892), NLM digitised text; Duke letter list (Penn guide).

entries.headline: The mayor orders the streets cleaned
entries.digest: Clarkson wrote to the city commissioners ordering the streets and wharves cleared of filth, a measure grounded in the belief that rotting matter bred the fever. It was the city government's first act in the epidemic.
entries.source_note: Carey, A Short Account of the Malignant Fever, 4th ed. (16 Jan 1794), NLM digitised text; American Heritage.

entries.headline: A fever of the malignant kind in Water Street
entries.digest: Drinker recorded that a fever was prevailing in the city, worst in Water Street between Race and Arch. She also noted the rumour that it came from damaged coffee and fish stored at a merchant's wharf. Within days her pages began to fill with names of the dead.
entries.quote: a fever prevails in the city, particularly in Water Street
entries.source_note: Drinker diary as quoted by Philadelphia Yearly Meeting; exact day within 23–30 Aug not confirmed.

entries.headline: The College of Physicians drafts rules
entries.digest: Rush told Julia the fever had spread far beyond Water Street and that the scene put him in mind of the plague. The College of Physicians had met and drafted public directions for the mayor. He asked her to keep the children in New Jersey and to pray for him.
entries.quote: the fever has assumed a most alarming appearance
entries.source_note: Old Family Letters Relating to the Yellow Fever (Philadelphia: Lippincott, 1892), NLM digitised text; Duke letter of 25–26 Aug.

entries.headline: Bells silenced, carts full of departing families
entries.digest: Carey dates the College of Physicians' address to 26 August and the start of mass removal to about the 25th. After the address the church bells, which had tolled for every funeral, were stopped. On the 29th the mayor banned bonfires in the streets.
entries.source_note: Carey, A Short Account of the Malignant Fever, 4th ed. (16 Jan 1794), NLM digitised text.

entries.headline: Bush Hill seized as a fever hospital
entries.digest: The Guardians of the Poor took possession of Bush Hill, an empty mansion once rented by Vice-President Adams, after neighbours drove off attempts to open a hospital nearer the city. It began as a place to put the friendless sick, with little staff and no order.
entries.source_note: Carey, A Short Account of the Malignant Fever, 4th ed. (16 Jan 1794), NLM digitised text.

entries.headline: Everybody who can is flying
entries.digest: Jefferson told Madison a malignant fever had risen from the filth of Water Street and that about seventy had died two days before. He listed the symptoms and the falling death rate among the sick. He had sent his daughter away but still went into town daily, and feared the countryside's panic could bring famine.
entries.quote: everybody who can is flying from the city
entries.source_note: Jefferson to Madison, 1 Sept 1793, Founders Online; phrase as quoted by Poplar Forest.

entries.headline: Thirty-eight dead in eleven families
entries.digest: Rush counted thirty-eight deaths in eleven Water Street families in nine days. Funerals now went to the grave with only a handful of followers.
entries.quote: Thirty eight persons have died in eleven families
entries.source_note: Old Family Letters Relating to the Yellow Fever (Philadelphia: Lippincott, 1892), NLM digitised text.

entries.headline: Twenty-nine out of thirty
entries.digest: After visiting nearly a hundred patients, Rush claimed that his purge of calomel and jalap saved twenty-nine of every thirty patients who took it on the first day. He complained that rival physicians were attacking him. The claim, made in exhaustion and certainty, became the core of a feud that outlived the epidemic.
entries.quote: I now save 29 out of 30
entries.source_note: Old Family Letters Relating to the Yellow Fever (Philadelphia: Lippincott, 1892), NLM digitised text.

entries.headline: The president checks on a sick secretary
entries.digest: Washington wrote to Hamilton, who feared he had the prevailing fever, hoping the fear was groundless and noting that the disorder seemed less malignant. He invited the Hamiltons to dine if health allowed. Four days later he left the city.
entries.source_note: Washington to Hamilton, 6 Sept 1793, Founders Online.

entries.headline: The African brethren supply the nurses
entries.digest: In a postscript Rush told Julia that the city's Black residents now furnished nurses for most of his patients. He believed, wrongly, that people of African descent were largely spared the fever, and had urged their leaders to help on that ground.
entries.quote: They furnish nurses to most of my patients.
entries.source_note: Old Family Letters Relating to the Yellow Fever (Philadelphia: Lippincott, 1892), NLM digitised text (postscript dated 6 or 7 Sept in different summaries).

entries.headline: Answering the call in the papers
entries.digest: Early in September a public appeal asked for help, and Jones and Allen called on the mayor the next day. Rush, knowing both could bleed, asked them to attend the sick and taught them his method. They also hired men to remove and bury the dead, whom no one else would touch.
entries.quote: Early in September, a solicitation appeared in the public papers
entries.source_note: Jones and Allen, A Narrative of the Proceedings of the Black People (1794), NLM digitised text. Exact days not given.

entries.headline: Back in the city to load a ship
entries.digest: Breck had come back from Bristol on the 8th to see a ship loaded for Liverpool and spent the 9th on business in streets where forty-five deaths were reported that day. The Vicomte de Noailles, a French émigré, urged him to get out. He recalled the date decades later.
entries.source_note: Breck, Recollections (1877), pp. 193–96; memoir written later.

entries.headline: The president leaves
entries.digest: Washington left with Martha and the children, who would not stay in a house the fever nearly surrounded, and reached Mount Vernon on the 14th. He later explained the timing to Tobias Lear, whose wife had died that summer.
entries.quote: We remained in Philadelphia until the 10th.
entries.source_note: Washington to Lear, 25 Sept 1793, as quoted by Colonial Williamsburg.

entries.headline: A hundred patients in a day
entries.digest: Rush marvelled that he was still well after prescribing for more than a hundred patients; forty were said to have been buried that day. He kept seeing the poor, remembering a dream he had had in 1780. He praised the African nurses and attacked physicians who rejected mercury.
entries.quote: Forty persons it is said have been buried this day
entries.source_note: Old Family Letters Relating to the Yellow Fever (Philadelphia: Lippincott, 1892), NLM digitised text; Duke catalogue description of the letter.

entries.headline: An appeal for volunteers
entries.digest: With the Guardians of the Poor nearly all fled, sick or dead, Clarkson published an address calling for citizens to help. Two days later a meeting produced only ten volunteers.
entries.source_note: Carey, A Short Account of the Malignant Fever, 4th ed. (16 Jan 1794), NLM digitised text.

entries.headline: A cabinet officer advertises his cure
entries.digest: Hamilton wrote to the College of Physicians, printed the same day in the Federal Gazette, that he had been violently attacked but was now out of danger thanks to Dr Edward Stevens. Stevens's treatment, he said, differed essentially from the common practice and made the disease little more dangerous than ordinary fevers. His wife had caught it from him and was also mending.
entries.quote: compleatly out of danger
entries.source_note: Hamilton to the College of Physicians, [11 Sept 1793], Founders Online.

entries.headline: Banks shut, clerks gone
entries.digest: Jefferson told Madison the fever spread faster, now in every quarter, with about thirty deaths a day. Most offices were closing, the banks shut that day, and all but one of his clerks had gone. He noted that 'H.' had truly had the fever and was out of danger, and planned to leave within days.
entries.quote: All flying who can
entries.source_note: Jefferson to Madison, 12 Sept 1793, Founders Online.

entries.headline: A week of names
entries.digest: Day by day Drinker wrote down who was reported dead: a widow near her brother-in-law, a miller's son buried at Chestnut Hill, a clergyman, Friends and neighbours, a husband and wife together. The entries are lists more than reflections, as if writing the names were the work to be done.
entries.source_note: Drinker journal, 12–18 Sept 1793, from 'Genealogical Gleanings from the Journal of Elizabeth Drinker' (Pennsylvania Vital Records I), via Ancestral Sightings.

entries.headline: A government of volunteers
entries.digest: A meeting under the mayor borrowed $1,500 and formed the committee that governed the city for the next two months, among them Carey, Girard and Helm. It met daily, hired carts, nurses and coffin-makers, and later opened a house for orphans.
entries.source_note: Carey, 4th ed.; Library Company finding aid; title page of the Minutes (1794).

entries.headline: Two merchants take over the hospital
entries.digest: Girard and Peter Helm offered to manage Bush Hill and began that afternoon. They found a hospital neglected by drunken attendants and set about cleaning it, organising nurses and sorting the sick from the convalescent. Within days the managers had hired nine women nurses, ten men attendants and a matron.
entries.source_note: Carey, 4th ed. (date of offer); staffing figure from committee records as summarised in secondary accounts.

entries.headline: The doctor falls ill
entries.digest: In a letter begun on the 15th Rush wrote that the disease touched nearly every family and that life and health felt like daily miracles. Next day he added that he had had an attack himself, bled and purged it, and took his recovery as proof that his treatment made the fever little worse than a cold.
entries.quote: Life and health become every day more and more a miracle
entries.source_note: Old Family Letters Relating to the Yellow Fever (Philadelphia: Lippincott, 1892), NLM digitised text.

entries.headline: The Secretary of State leaves
entries.digest: Jefferson and his daughter left for Virginia earlier than he had planned, a week after the President. The federal government had now effectively dispersed.
entries.source_note: Poplar Forest, 'Jefferson's response'; date of departure not confirmed to the day.

entries.headline: Not contagious, only epidemic
entries.digest: At Bush Hill, engaged by Girard, Devèze treated patients with moderate bleeding adjusted to the case, camphor, blisters and bark, and avoided early purges and mercury. He opened many bodies and, handling them without falling ill, concluded that the fever was not contagious and had arisen in the country itself.
entries.source_note: Devèze, Enquiry (1794), NLM text; start date at Bush Hill not given.

entries.headline: A pupil dies in the house
entries.digest: Johnny Stall, one of the apprentices who mixed and carried Rush's medicines, died at about half past noon. Two days later another pupil, Alston, was dead. Rush kept writing about grateful families as if to hold the losses in balance.
entries.quote: Johnny Stall breathed his last
entries.source_note: Old Family Letters Relating to the Yellow Fever (Philadelphia: Lippincott, 1892), NLM digitised text.

entries.headline: His sister dies
entries.digest: Rush's sister Rebecca, who had kept house and nursed patients while he worked, died that afternoon and was buried in a plain coffin. He called her a martyr to humanity. Later he wrote that she had given her life to save his.
entries.quote: my dear sister breathed her last
entries.source_note: Old Family Letters Relating to the Yellow Fever (Philadelphia: Lippincott, 1892), NLM digitised text.

entries.headline: Thirty sick visited, twelve soon buried
entries.digest: Helmuth's journal for 5 October lists about thirty sick people he visited; twelve were buried within days. That week his congregation lost about 130 members. Gravediggers could make twenty to twenty-six graves a day, so some burials were done at night, often followed only by the hearse driver.
entries.source_note: Helmuth, Short Account (1794), quoting his journal; NLM text.

entries.headline: Calm after a night of grief
entries.digest: Rush reported the death of Mrs Kepple and that another woman was past hope. He had stopped answering most calls and recorded a prayer of submission.
entries.quote: Not my will, but thine be done.
entries.source_note: Old Family Letters Relating to the Yellow Fever (Philadelphia: Lippincott, 1892), NLM digitised text.

entries.headline: Two thousand dead, and the fever returns
entries.digest: The mayor told Rush that nearly 2,000 had died since the fever appeared. That evening Rush's own fever came back and kept him indoors for days. He railed against colleagues who gave bark and laudanum after one or two bleedings.
entries.quote: nearly 2000 persons had died in our city
entries.source_note: Old Family Letters Relating to the Yellow Fever (Philadelphia: Lippincott, 1892), NLM digitised text; letters of 10–11 Oct.

entries.headline: The worst day: 119 burials
entries.digest: Carey's tables put the peak at 11 October, with 119 deaths, followed by 111 and 104 on the next two days. The week of 7 to 13 October was the deadliest of the epidemic.
entries.source_note: Carey, A Short Account of the Malignant Fever, 4th ed. (16 Jan 1794), NLM digitised text (daily table). Week total of 711 from secondary summaries.

entries.headline: Neighbours and a committee man
entries.digest: Drinker listed more deaths she had heard of: an elderly Friend, two brothers of one family, Daniel Offley, the widow Kepley, and another daughter of James Starr. Offley was one of the five members of the mayor's committee who died.
entries.source_note: Drinker journal, 11 Oct 1793 (Genealogical Gleanings, p. 608, via Ancestral Sightings); Carey, 4th ed., list of deceased members.

entries.headline: A frost that memory supplied
entries.digest: Breck remembered about a thousand deaths between 1 and 12 October, ended by a hard frost on the 12th. The contemporary tables show the peak on the 11th but a slow decline and no killing frost until later; it is a vivid memory, compressed.
entries.source_note: Breck, Recollections (1877); contrast Carey's tables and Rush's 11 Nov letter.

entries.headline: Where can Congress meet?
entries.digest: Washington wrote to Madison, Randolph and Wolcott asking whether he had power to convene Congress somewhere other than Philadelphia and where it might go. The epidemic had become a constitutional problem.
entries.source_note: Washington to Madison, to Randolph and to Wolcott, 14 Oct 1793, Founders Online (titles seen; contents summarised from the editors' notes).

entries.headline: Servants deserting, the sick sent to Bush Hill
entries.digest: Rush credited his Black servant Marcus with nursing him through the nights. He wrote that half the servants in the city had left their masters, and some of the sick had died neglected or been sent to the hospital at Bush Hill.
entries.quote: Half the servants in the city have deserted their masters
entries.source_note: Old Family Letters Relating to the Yellow Fever (Philadelphia: Lippincott, 1892), NLM digitised text. Marcus left no record of his own.

entries.headline: A thousand in the Potter's Field
entries.digest: Riding out for the first time since the 10th, Rush saw more people in the streets. He reported that upwards of a thousand had been buried in the Potter's Field, the burial ground of the poor and the strangers.
entries.quote: Upwards of 1000 persons have been buried in that grave yard
entries.source_note: Old Family Letters Relating to the Yellow Fever (Philadelphia: Lippincott, 1892), NLM digitised text.

entries.headline: The disease visibly declines
entries.digest: With cooler weather Rush wrote that the disease was declining everywhere. In another note he said he was accused of claiming that the fever had been generated in the city, a position he did not abandon.
entries.quote: The disease visibly and universally declines.
entries.source_note: Old Family Letters Relating to the Yellow Fever (Philadelphia: Lippincott, 1892), NLM digitised text.

entries.headline: Jones and Allen report
entries.digest: Allen and Jones called on Rush and told him how many poor patients they had treated with his remedies. He believed they had saved between two and three hundred lives.
entries.quote: saved the lives of between two and three hundred persons
entries.source_note: Old Family Letters Relating to the Yellow Fever (Philadelphia: Lippincott, 1892), NLM digitised text.

entries.headline: A white flag over the hospital
entries.digest: By the end of October admissions at Bush Hill had fallen sharply, and a white flag was raised over the hospital to signal that the danger was passing. Rush, by contrast, wrote on 3 November that two-fifths of all the sick sent there had died.
entries.source_note: Secondary summary of committee records (white flag); Rush letter of 3 Nov, Old Family Letters Relating to the Yellow Fever (Philadelphia: Lippincott, 1892), NLM digitised text.

entries.headline: Citizens crowding back
entries.digest: On the anniversary of his sister's death a month before, Rush reported that citizens were crowding into town every day, and that some returning were falling ill.
entries.quote: The citizens are crowding into town every day.
entries.source_note: Old Family Letters Relating to the Yellow Fever (Philadelphia: Lippincott, 1892), NLM digitised text.

entries.headline: Almost entirely disappeared
entries.digest: Back near the capital, Jefferson told Madison that the fever in Philadelphia had almost entirely disappeared and that people were returning.
entries.quote: the fever in Philadelphia has almost entirely disappeared
entries.source_note: Jefferson to Madison, 9 Nov 1793, as quoted by Poplar Forest.

entries.headline: Still no frost
entries.digest: Rush's practice was growing again and he would attend the hospital. He noted a woman who seemed to have caught the fever from an old coat, and that no frost had yet touched the city's gardens.
entries.quote: as yet no frost has touched them
entries.source_note: Old Family Letters Relating to the Yellow Fever (Philadelphia: Lippincott, 1892), NLM digitised text.

entries.headline: The first history goes to press
entries.digest: Carey entered his Short Account for copyright and dated its preface while the city was still returning. It held that the fever had most unquestionably been imported from the West Indies and that the newly settled French had largely escaped it.
entries.quote: has most unquestionably been imported from the West Indies
entries.source_note: Carey, A Short Account of the Malignant Fever, 4th ed. (16 Jan 1794), NLM digitised text (copyright and preface dates).

entries.headline: Safe to return
entries.digest: The mayor's committee announced that people could return without danger, while urging that houses be cleaned and aired first. Stagecoaches had resumed the day before.
entries.source_note: Secondary summaries of committee notices; Library Company finding aid ('middle of November').

entries.headline: The paragraph on the nurses
entries.digest: In the second edition Carey wrote that some of the vilest Black people had seized the chance to impose on the sick, with nurses extorting two to five dollars a night, and that some had been caught plundering houses. He added that extortion was by no means confined to Black people and praised Jones, Allen and Gray.
entries.quote: some of the vilest of the blacks
entries.source_note: Carey, A Short Account of the Malignant Fever, 4th ed. (16 Jan 1794), NLM digitised text; second-edition preface dated 23 Nov. Wording quoted from the 4th edition.

entries.headline: A list of 4,041 names
entries.digest: The fourth edition added a list of names of the dead from 1 August, compiled from church books and house-to-house inquiry, totalling 4,041. The largest single figures were the Potter's Field, 1,334, and the German Lutherans, 641. Carey warned the list was not complete.
entries.source_note: Carey, A Short Account of the Malignant Fever, 4th ed. (16 Jan 1794), NLM digitised text, list and burial-ground table.

entries.headline: An answer, with accounts
entries.digest: Jones and Allen published their reply. They named nurses who had refused pay, such as the widow Sarah Bass and Caesar Cranchal, and told of a white man who threatened to shoot them for carrying a corpse past his house. They printed their accounts, showing they were about £177 out of pocket, and noted that 305 Black people had been buried in 1793 against 67 the year before.
entries.quote: I will not sell my life for money.
entries.source_note: Jones and Allen, A Narrative of the Proceedings of the Black People (1794), NLM digitised text; copyright 23 Jan 1794; mayor's certificate of the same date.

claims.claim: Identifies the cluster of Water Street fevers as bilious remitting yellow fever, like 1762
claims.evidence: Rush, Account (1794); his letter of 21 Aug

claims.claim: Twelve already dead of a malignant fever in Water Street
Records the rumour that the fever came from damaged coffee and fish on a wharf (local-origin view)
claims.evidence: Drinker diary, as quoted by Philadelphia Yearly Meeting

claims.claim: About 70 dead in two days; deaths among the sick down from three in four to one in three
Claims his calomel-and-jalap purge saves 29 of 30 treated on the first day
Believes Black people largely escape the fever; enlists them as nurses (belief later refuted by the burial figures)
claims.evidence: Rush letters of early Sept; Jones and Allen, Narrative

claims.claim: Recovery under Stevens's bark-and-cold-bath treatment, offered as a rival to Rush's depletion
Not contagious but epidemic, arising locally; based on many autopsies at Bush Hill
About 130 of his congregation died in one week
claims.evidence: Helmuth, Short Account (1794), quoting his journal

claims.claim: Nearly 2,000 deaths since the fever appeared (mayor's count, relayed by Rush)
Peak of 119 deaths in a day; 111 and 104 on the next two days
claims.evidence: Carey, Short Account, 4th ed., daily table

claims.claim: Two-fifths of all the sick sent to Bush Hill died
Fever imported from the West Indies (contagionist position), against Rush's local-origin view
4,041 named dead, 1 Aug to mid-Dec; by month 325 Aug, 1,442 Sept, 1,993 Oct, 118 Nov; later estimates about 5,000 of some 50,000
305 Black people buried in 1793 against 67 in 1792; they bled upwards of 800 people
Burial work cost £411 against £233 received: a loss of about £177
claims.evidence: Jones and Allen, Narrative, account of expenses

convergences.label: The fever is named
convergences.note: On the same Monday Rush was naming the disease at a dying woman's bedside and Helmuth was called to a man who would be dead by morning. Carey later dated the first deaths that people talked about to those two days. Drinker's diary had the rumour of rotten coffee within the week. Each later read the same days as the start of a different story: a medical diagnosis, a divine visitation, a public alarm.

convergences.label: Counting the first wave
convergences.note: Jefferson's seventy dead in two days and Rush's thirty-eight in eleven families are written the same Sunday. One counts for the cabinet and the countryside's panic, the other house by house.

convergences.label: The president leaves; the doctor sees a hundred
convergences.note: Washington rode out on 10 September. That day Rush saw more than a hundred patients and forty were buried, Clarkson appealed for volunteers, and Breck had just spent a day on the wharves. Next day Hamilton announced his cure in the newspaper, as a rival method.

convergences.label: The city empties
convergences.note: Banks shut and clerks fled, Jefferson wrote; Drinker began a week of lists of the dead; the mayor's call for volunteers drew only ten men to the meeting that day. Flight, mourning and improvisation sit on the same page of the calendar.

convergences.label: A government of volunteers
convergences.note: The committee formed on the 14th; on the 15th Girard and Helm took on Bush Hill, where Devèze would practise the cautious French method, while across town Rush fell ill and treated himself with his own purges.

convergences.label: The worst week
convergences.note: Carey's table peaks at 119 on 11 October. Drinker writes down Daniel Offley and the widow Kepley among the dead; Rush, relapsed, had recorded Mrs Kepple's death on the 9th. Helmuth's congregation lost 130 that week. Breck, decades later, remembered a frost on the 12th that the records do not show.

convergences.label: Returning
convergences.note: As the cold came, Rush saw citizens crowding back, Bush Hill flew its white flag, and the government gathered at Germantown. Jefferson wrote on 9 November that the fever had almost entirely gone; Rush on the 11th was still waiting for frost.

convergences.label: Who served, and who is blamed
convergences.note: A week after Carey's fourth edition gave 4,041 names, Jones and Allen published their reply with a certificate from Mayor Clarkson. The quarrel set the official chronicle against the testimony of the people who had carried the dead.

ties.note: Rush asked them to help, taught them to bleed and purge, and recorded their report of 29 October. His mistaken belief in Black immunity is part of why they were asked.
Their Narrative is a point-by-point reply to Carey's passage on Black nurses, which they called partial and censorious.
They called on the mayor in early September; in January 1794 he certified their conduct for the Narrative.
Carey sat on the mayor's committee and drew on its records for his history.
Girard and Helm volunteered to the mayor's committee to run Bush Hill on 15 September.
Girard engaged Devèze, a fellow Frenchman from the Caribbean trade world, for Bush Hill; Devèze praised Girard's devotion in print.
Rush's heavy purging and bleeding against Devèze's cautious method; on 25 October Rush wrote scornfully of the French physicians.
Hamilton's public letter promoted Stevens's bark-and-bath treatment as the alternative to Rush's; the choice of cure became identified with party.
Cabinet rivals; Jefferson's letters to Madison report Hamilton's illness with scepticism about how serious it was.
Washington wrote to Hamilton on 6 and 25 September about his illness and recovery and the reassembly of the government.
On 10 October the mayor gave Rush the count of nearly 2,000 dead, which Rush passed to his wife.
Both recorded the deaths of the same neighbours in the same week of October, Rush the widow Kepple on the 9th, Drinker the widow Kepley on the 11th.
Carey's burial table gave the Lutherans 641 dead, the largest count for any congregation, the losses Helmuth recorded at the bedside.
Breck's memoir singles out Girard's work in the hospital.

threads_out.note: On 9 January 1793, eight months before the fever, Jean-Pierre Blanchard made the first balloon ascent in America from the prison yard on Walnut Street, Philadelphia, watched by Washington. The same crowds and the same president fill this chapter.

The city of the Constitutional Convention, and two of its central figures, Washington and Hamilton, are in this chapter six years later. The emptied capital forced Washington to ask whether the Constitution let him summon Congress elsewhere.

The refugees from Saint-Domingue, Devèze and Girard's French world, and émigrés such as the Vicomte de Noailles in Breck's memoir link Philadelphia's plague year to the French and Haitian revolutions.

The argument in 1793 between local miasma (Rush, Devèze) and imported contagion (Carey and the College) is the argument Snow entered in London sixty years later. Neither side in 1793 suspected the mosquito, Aedes aegypti, shown to carry yellow fever by Finlay and Reed's commission (1881–1900), whose breeding the frost ended.
Philadelphia was again the worst-hit large American city in the 1918 influenza, with carts collecting the dead and volunteers improvising care. It was the city's second great emptying.
